text: PART 7 - ELITE: how top labs and practitioners do it
7.0 Concept

What: the habits that separate a demo from work a frontier lab, a health-AI company or a strong reviewer would trust: proving there is no test leakage, proving a gain is not noise, proving the judge agrees with humans, scoring against explicit criteria, rolling out model versions without downtime, and documenting everything in a model card.

Why: in interviews and in real teams, "accuracy went from 61% to 64%" is worthless until you can answer: was the test set contaminated, is 3 points significant on 500 questions, who graded it and how reliable is the grader, and can you roll it back?
When: before you claim any result anywhere (CV, README, interview, paper).
Harder than Part 6 because: the work is statistical and methodological, not just engineering, and it can (and should) prove your own earlier claims wrong.

text: SECTION 7.2 - Prove there is no test leakage (near-duplicate contamination check)
WHERE: VS Code Terminal, folder ~/-MEDSCRIPTAI/scripts, (.venv-eval) active
GOAL: the number of test questions that are near-copies of training questions (should be 0).
Step 1. Run:
python 04_contamination_check.py
You should see: qa test rows= 500 near-duplicates of training rows= 0 (0.0%) and the same for notes and summary.
FILE scripts/04_contamination_check.py:

"""Elite check: is any TEST question a near-copy of a TRAINING question? (13-gram overlap, GPT-3 paper style)

Exact-match de-duplication (step 2) misses near-copies: the same question with one word changed.
Medical exams share stock phrases ("is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of",
lab panels), so ONE shared 13-gram proves nothing. We flag a test question only when at least
50% of its 13-grams come from a SINGLE training question.
"""
import re
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
from common import SFT, read_jsonl

N = 13                       # n-gram length in words
THRESHOLD = 0.5              # share of the test question's n-grams found in one training question


def grams(text):
    text = text.split("\n\nOptions:")[0]                 # compare the question stem, not the option labels
    words = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9]+", text.lower())
    return {" ".join(words[i:i + N]) for i in range(len(words) - N + 1)}


for task in ["qa", "notes", "summary"]:
    index = defaultdict(set)                             # n-gram -> ids of training rows containing it
    path = SFT / f"{task}_train.jsonl"
    if path.exists():
        for row_id, row in enumerate(read_jsonl(path)):
            for g in grams(row["messages"][1]["content"]):
                index[g].add(row_id)
    test = read_jsonl(SFT / f"{task}_test.jsonl")
    flagged = []
    for row in test:
        test_grams = grams(row["messages"][1]["content"])
        per_train_row = Counter(i for g in test_grams for i in index.get(g, ()))
        best = per_train_row.most_common(1)[0][1] if per_train_row else 0
        if test_grams and best / len(test_grams) >= THRESHOLD:
            flagged.append(row["messages"][1]["content"][:110].replace("\n", " "))
    print(f"{task:8} test rows={len(test):4}  near-duplicates of training rows={len(flagged):3} "
          f"({len(flagged) / max(len(test), 1):.1%})")
    for text in flagged[:3]:
        print("   e.g.", text)

rows: n-gram length, as in the GPT-3 contamination analysis
flag a test question if at least half of its 13-grams come from ONE training question
lower-case words, cut the "Options:" block, return the set of all 13-word windows
inverted index: 13-gram -> ids of training rows that contain it
`per_train_row = Counter(i for g in test_grams for i in index.get(g, ()))`
for one test question, how many of its 13-grams each training row shares
the share coming from the single most similar training row

text: What we learned while building this (a real elite lesson): the first version flagged 13% of QA test questions as contaminated after exact de-duplication. Inspection showed false positives: exam boilerplate ("which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management", standard lab panels, "is brought to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of"). Counting a single shared 13-gram over-reports leakage in templated domains; requiring that half of a question comes from one training row fixed it, and a planted near-copy (one word changed) was still caught.

Watch out: this checks YOUR training data. The base model's pre-training data may already contain MedQA (it is public). That is why Med-PaLM 2, HealthBench and MedHELM also evaluate on new, private or expert-written items. Say this in interviews.
CHECKPOINT: 0 near-duplicates (or a short list you then remove from training and re-train).
SECTION 7.3 - Prove a gain is real (paired bootstrap confidence interval)
WHERE: VS Code Terminal, folder ~/-MEDSCRIPTAI/scripts, (.venv-eval) active
GOAL: a 95% confidence interval for "DPO accuracy minus SFT accuracy".
Step 1. Run:
python 33_significance.py --a qa --b qa-dpo
Step 2. Also compare base vs SFT:
python 33_significance.py --a base --b qa
You should see: accuracy qa=... qa-dpo=... diff=+0.0xx, a 95% CI such as [-0.010, +0.052] and either SIGNIFICANT or NOT significant.
FILE scripts/33_significance.py:

"""Elite check: is model B REALLY better than model A, or is it noise? Paired bootstrap on QA accuracy.

python scripts/33_significance.py --a qa --b qa-dpo
"""
import argparse
import random
from common import OUT, read_jsonl

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--a", required=True)
p.add_argument("--b", required=True)
p.add_argument("--rounds", type=int, default=10000)
args = p.parse_args()


def correct(row):
    pred = row["prediction"] or ""
    letter = pred.split("Answer:", 1)[1].strip()[:1].upper() if "Answer:" in pred else None
    return int(letter == row["answer_letter"])


a = [correct(r) for r in read_jsonl(OUT / "preds" / "qa" / f"{args.a}.jsonl")]
b = [correct(r) for r in read_jsonl(OUT / "preds" / "qa" / f"{args.b}.jsonl")]
n = min(len(a), len(b))
diffs = []
rng = random.Random(0)
for _ in range(args.rounds):
    idx = [rng.randrange(n) for _ in range(n)]          # resample the SAME questions for both models
    diffs.append(sum(b[i] - a[i] for i in idx) / n)
diffs.sort()
low, high = diffs[int(0.025 * args.rounds)], diffs[int(0.975 * args.rounds)]
observed = (sum(b[:n]) - sum(a[:n])) / n
print(f"accuracy {args.a}={sum(a[:n]) / n:.3f}  {args.b}={sum(b[:n]) / n:.3f}  diff={observed:+.3f}")
print(f"95% CI of the difference: [{low:+.3f}, {high:+.3f}]")
print("SIGNIFICANT" if low > 0 or high < 0 else "NOT significant: the CI contains 0, do not claim an improvement")

rows: 1 if the predicted letter equals the gold letter, else 0
per-question correctness for the two models, on the SAME 500 questions
a bootstrap sample: draw 500 question indices with replacement
`diffs.append(sum(b[i] - a[i] for i in idx) / n)`
the accuracy difference on that resampled test set; PAIRED because both models are scored on the same resampled questions
repeat 10,000 times to get the distribution of the difference
the middle 95% of the differences = the confidence interval
if the interval does not contain 0, the difference is unlikely to be noise

text: Rule of thumb you should be able to say in an interview: on 500 multiple-choice questions, the 95% interval of a single accuracy is about +/- 4 points, so a 2-point gain is usually NOT significant; paired tests are tighter because both models share the hard questions.
CHECKPOINT: you can state each comparison as "diff X, 95% CI [L, H]".
SECTION 7.4 - Prove the judge is trustworthy (agreement with your own labels)
WHERE: VS Code Terminal and WinSCP (or VS Code editor), folder ~/-MEDSCRIPTAI/scripts, (.venv-eval) active
GOAL: Cohen's kappa between the LLM judge and you on 30 pairwise comparisons.
Step 1. Create the label sheet:
python 35_judge_agreement.py --judge-file ../outputs/reports/judge_qa_pairwise_qa-dpo_vs_qa.json
You should see: fill the 'human' column in .../outputs/reports/human_labels.csv, then run this script again
Step 2. Show the two answers for item i (repeat for i = 0..29; change I_NUMBER):

python -c "import json;a=[json.loads(l) for l in open('../outputs/preds/qa/qa-dpo.jsonl')];b=[json.loads(l) for l in open('../outputs/preds/qa/qa.jsonl')];i=I_NUMBER;print(a[i]['prompt'],'

REFERENCE:',a[i]['reference'],'

qa-dpo:',a[i]['prediction'],'

qa:',b[i]['prediction'])"
Step 3. Open outputs/reports/human_labels.csv in VS Code (Explorer panel) and type qa-dpo, qa or tie in the human column for each row you judged. Save with Ctrl+S.
Step 4. Run again:
python 35_judge_agreement.py --judge-file ../outputs/reports/judge_qa_pairwise_qa-dpo_vs_qa.json
You should see: items=30 agreement=0.xx Cohen's kappa=0.xx and the interpretation line.
FILE scripts/35_judge_agreement.py:

"""Elite check: can you trust the LLM judge? Compare its pairwise verdicts with YOUR labels (Cohen's kappa).

1) Open outputs/reports/human_labels.csv (created on first run) and fill the 'human' column
   with the model name you prefer, or 'tie', for each row (read the two answers in the preds files).
2) Run again: python scripts/35_judge_agreement.py --judge-file outputs/reports/judge_qa_pairwise_qa-dpo_vs_qa.json
"""
import argparse
import csv
import json
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path
from common import OUT

p = argparse.ArgumentParser()
p.add_argument("--judge-file", required=True)
p.add_argument("--n", type=int, default=30, help="how many items you will label by hand")
a = p.parse_args()

judge = json.loads(Path(a.judge_file).read_text())["per_item"][: a.n]
labels = OUT / "reports" / "human_labels.csv"
if not labels.exists():                                     # first run: make the sheet for you to fill
    with labels.open("w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["i", "human"])
        w.writerows([[i, ""] for i in range(len(judge))])
    print(f"fill the 'human' column in {labels}, then run this script again")
    raise SystemExit

human = {int(r["i"]): r["human"].strip() for r in csv.DictReader(labels.open()) if r["human"].strip()}
pairs = [(judge[i], h) for i, h in human.items() if i < len(judge)]
n = len(pairs)
observed = sum(j == h for j, h in pairs) / n                 # raw agreement
jc, hc = Counter(j for j, _ in pairs), Counter(h for _, h in pairs)
expected = sum(jc[k] * hc[k] for k in set(jc) | set(hc)) / (n * n)   # agreement by pure chance
kappa = (observed - expected) / (1 - expected) if expected < 1 else 1.0
print(f"items={n}  agreement={observed:.2f}  Cohen's kappa={kappa:.2f}")
print("kappa > 0.6 = judge is usable; 0.4-0.6 = use with care; < 0.4 = do not trust this judge")

rows: the judge's verdict per item, saved by 32_judge.py
first run only creates the sheet for you
your labels; empty rows are ignored
raw agreement: how often you and the judge said the same
agreement you would get by chance given how often each of you uses each label
Cohen's kappa: agreement beyond chance. 1 = perfect, 0 = no better than chance

text: A lesson from testing: with a judge that always answered "qa-dpo", raw agreement was 0.80 but kappa was 0.00. High agreement can be meaningless when one label dominates; that is exactly why kappa exists.

Watch out: you are not a physician. For a real medical product the labels must come from clinicians (HealthBench used 262 physicians). For this project, be transparent: "judge-human agreement measured on 30 items by the author".
CHECKPOINT: you can report kappa with its interpretation.

SECTION 7.6 - Zero-downtime adapter rollout and rollback (canary)
WHERE: VS Code Terminal, folder ~/-MEDSCRIPTAI, Compose stack from Section 6.7 running
GOAL: switch task qa from qa-dpo to a new adapter version without restarting vLLM, then roll back in seconds.
Step 1. Ask vLLM (from inside the api container, because vLLM's port is not published) which adapters it serves:
docker compose -f deploy/docker-compose.yml exec api python -c "import urllib.request,json; print([m['id'] for m in json.load(urllib.request.urlopen('http://vllm:8000/v1/models'))['data']])"
You should see: ['base', 'qa', 'notes', 'summary', 'qa-dpo'].
Step 2. Change the route for qa in deploy/.env (open the file and add this line, then save):
MODEL_QA=qa
Step 3. Recreate ONLY the api container (vLLM keeps running and keeps its GPU memory):
cd deploy && docker compose --env-file .env up -d api && cd ..
Step 4. Check the route:

curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/v1/generate -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "X-API-Key: $(grep ^API_KEY deploy/.env | cut -d= -f2)" -d '{"task":"qa","input":"Which vitamin deficiency causes scurvy?

Options:
A) A
B) B12
C) C
D) D"}' | jq -r .model
You should see: qa (the SFT adapter now answers). Rollback = set MODEL_QA=qa-dpo and repeat Step 3.

rows: send a small share of traffic to the new version and watch metrics before switching everyone (with two API deployments behind a load balancer, or a percentage router in the API)
returning to the previous version; here one variable and a 2-second container restart
adapters are tiny and vLLM can host many at once; the expensive base model never reloads

text: Watch out: the Compose file does not enable VLLM_ALLOW_RUNTIME_LORA_UPDATING (production safety). To add a brand-new adapter in Compose, add it to --lora-modules and recreate vllm, or enable runtime updates only on a private network.
CHECKPOINT: you switched and rolled back without vLLM restarting (docker compose ps shows vllm Up for the same duration).

FILE scripts/34_report.py:

"""Build outputs/reports/REPORT.md (paste it into your Hugging Face model card and your CV/portfolio)."""
import json
from pathlib import Path
from common import OUT

reports = OUT / "reports"
metrics = json.loads((reports / "metrics.json").read_text())
cols = ["n", "accuracy", "format_ok", "json_valid", "rougeL", "bertscore_f1"]
lines = ["# MedScriptAI evaluation report", "", "## Automatic metrics", "",
         "| task/model | " + " | ".join(cols) + " |", "|" + "---|" * (len(cols) + 1)]
for name, m in metrics.items():
    lines.append(f"| {name} | " + " | ".join(str(m.get(c, "-")) for c in cols) + " |")
lines += ["", "## LLM-as-a-judge", ""]
for path in sorted(reports.glob("judge_*.json")):
    lines.append(f"- **{path.stem.removeprefix('judge_')}**: `{json.dumps(json.loads(path.read_text()))}`")
lines += ["", "Judge: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Pairwise results use position swapping (a win must win in both orders).",
          "", "Built with Llama. Educational use only; not a medical device and not medical advice."]
(reports / "REPORT.md").write_text("\n".join(lines) + "\n")
print("\n".join(lines))

rows: the columns of the Markdown table
one table row per task/model; "-" where a metric does not apply
judge description, "Built with Llama", and the not-for-clinical-use statement

7.8 What elite teams would do next (pick one as your stretch goal)

items: **RL with verifiable rewards (GRPO).** For multiple-choice QA the reward is checkable (correct letter = 1). TRL's GRPOTrainer and Unsloth support it; this is the DeepSeek-R1 / Tulu 3 style of post-training (verify current TRL/Unsloth GRPO docs).
**Other preference losses.** Compare DPO with SimPO (loss_type="sigmoid_norm" in TRL), IPO, KTO or ORPO on the same pairs; report the significance test for each.
**Iterative on-policy DPO.** Regenerate pairs with the DPO model and train a second round; stop when the win rate stops moving.
**Serving efficiency.** FP8 or AWQ-quantised base model for serving, prefix caching for the long shared system prompt, speculative decoding; measure tokens/second and cost per 1,000 requests.
**Safety evaluation.** A red-team set (self-harm, dosage requests, emergencies) with expected refusals or escalation messages; track refusal rate next to helpfulness.

**Privacy and regulation.** Real clinical notes contain PHI: de-identify, keep traces private (self-hosted LangSmith or redaction), and know that software making clinical decisions is regulated (for example FDA "software as a medical device").

text: 7.9 Common mistake at this level

The mistake: running elite-looking analyses that are not tied to a decision: a kappa nobody reads, a CI computed on a different test set than the headline number, a contamination check run after the paper is written.

How to spot it: every analysis answers one question that would change what you ship or what you claim. Write the question first ("is DPO better than SFT on QA accuracy?"), then the analysis, then the decision ("ship qa-dpo" or "keep qa").
